metadata.title: Investigating preservice teachers’ emotions and dialogic teaching practices in simulation-based learning with artificial intelligence-powered virtual student agents

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study used a purposefully sampled convenience cohort of 22 preservice teachers from a single southeastern U.S. university and analyzed system-logged interaction records at the sentence level. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, and the analysis is not framed as population-representative estimation. Because the quantitative component relies on association rule mining (Apriori) over coded emotion and dialogic talk moves rather than PV-based achievement scaling, standard ILSA-style weighting variables are not applicable here. The analytic dataset was constructed by logging virtual-student interactions during 2–4 hour VR simulation sessions and then applying frequency thresholds (support = 0.01; lift = 1.2) to extract salient co-occurrence rules.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the dependent variables are coded teaching emotions and dialogic talk moves derived from VR simulation interaction logs and qualitative coding, not cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA PV framework. Missing-data handling is not reported because the study does not describe any imputation/deletion procedure for missing questionnaire items or PVs; instead, it reports association-rule mining over coded sentence-level events and triangulated qualitative evidence. This omission is best interpreted as a reporting gap for missingness in coded interaction data, but it is less consequential than in PV-based achievement analyses where missingness is typically handled explicitly.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Purposeful sampling of preservice teachers enrolled in math- or science-focused teacher education programs at a southeastern U.S. university; participants were 18+ and consented to an IRB-approved VR-supported simulation session lasting 2–4 hours. Participants voluntarily selected teaching topics across mathematics (numbers, algebra, measurement, geometry), physical science (e.g., gas laws), and biology (e.g., fungi). The quantitative unit of analysis was sentence-level coded interactions from system-logged chat and observed verbal/non-verbal reactions during the EVETeach simulation; association rule mining used emotion and dialogic talk codes with minimum support and lift thresholds.

main_findings.dataset_used: EVETeach VR simulation with AI-powered virtual students (TIMSS/AST fine-tuning; sentence-level coded emotions)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Descriptive counts: neutral n=404; joy n=371; satisfaction n=311; anxiety & uncertainty n=141; positive states n=791; negative states n=184. Association-rule thresholds: support ≥ 0.01; lift ≥ 1.2. Example rules: {Satisfaction, Frustration}→{Excitement} (support 0.01, lift 1.99); {Anger, Neutral}→{Anxiety and uncertainty} (support 0.02, lift 1.30); {Satisfaction, Anger}→{Joy} (support 0.01, lift 1.21); {Excitement, Satisfaction, Neutral}→{Frustration} (support 0.01, lift 1.72).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using EVETeach VR simulation data with AI-powered virtual students (sentence-level coded emotions), the study leveraged co-occurrence patterns among coded emotion states to characterize how preservice teachers’ emotions clustered during practice, finding that neutral, joy, and satisfaction were more frequent than negative emotions and that satisfaction was a key element linking negative to positive states (e.g., satisfaction with frustration/anger associated with excitement/joy). This indicates that designing AI virtual-student interactions that reliably elicit student progress may help preservice teachers regulate frustration and sustain positive engagement during dialogic teaching practice, though the association-rule approach does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: EVETeach VR simulation with AI-powered virtual students (TIMSS/AST fine-tuning; sentence-level coded dialogic talk moves)
main_findings.target_variable: Dialogic teacher talk patterns (coded talk moves by stage)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Frequency counts: probes n=370; orchestrates n=250; explores n=182; evaluates n=159; consensus-building stage n=940 vs initiation stage n=438. Association-rule thresholds: support ≥ 0.01; lift ≥ 1.2. Example rules: {Displays, Presents}→{Explores} (support 1.0, lift 3.68); {Displays, Probes}→{Explores, Orchestrates} (support 0.33, lift 5.31); {Builds on ideas, Acknowledges or praises, Evaluates}→{Orchestrates} (support 0.78, lift 1.79); {Builds on ideas, Counter-argues}→{Orchestrates} (support 0.57, lift 1.30); {Presents (in initiation stage)}→{Other} (support 0.22, lift 1.33); {Acknowledges or praises, Counter-argues}→{Presents (in consensus building stage)} (support 0.75, lift 3.45).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using EVETeach VR simulation data with AI-powered virtual students (sentence-level coded dialogic talk moves), the study leveraged co-occurrence patterns among talk-move codes to characterize how preservice teachers enacted dialogic practices across initiation and consensus-building stages, finding that probes and orchestrates were most frequent and that orchestrating was strongly associated with building on ideas (often alongside acknowledging/praising and evaluating) rather than with lecture-like presenting. This indicates that VR simulation design should scaffold preservice teachers toward idea uptake and probing in early discourse so they can orchestrate consensus later, while recognizing that association rules describe patterns of co-occurrence rather than causal impacts.

data.outcome_summary: This open-access Learning and Instruction study examined preservice teachers’ emotions and dialogic talk during VR-supported simulation-based teaching with AI-powered virtual student agents (EVETeach). The quantitative component used association rule mining with the Apriori algorithm on sentence-level coded interaction data, extracting co-occurrence patterns among emotion states (e.g., neutral, joy, satisfaction, anxiety/uncertainty) and dialogic talk moves (e.g., explores, probes, orchestrates) across initiation vs consensus-building stages. The study reports descriptive frequencies (e.g., neutral n=404; joy n=371; satisfaction n=311; anxiety/uncertainty n=141) and association-rule strength using support and lift (e.g., satisfaction/frustration→excitement lift=1.99; builds-on-ideas/counter-argues→orchestrates lift=1.30). No PV-based achievement outcomes, survey weights, or missing-data imputation/deletion procedures are described, and the association-rule approach cannot establish causal effects or temporal dynamics beyond co-occurrence. The findings nonetheless suggest design levers for AI virtual students that elicit progress and support idea uptake to promote emotionally balanced, ambitious dialogic teaching.
